column1: What is AWS Elastic Beanstalk (EB), and who is it best suited for?
column2:
- A PaaS (platform as a service): AWS handles the infrastructure, you manage the code
- Developer-focused: you provide app code and EB handles the environment/infrastructure
- Good for small developer teams and getting proofs of concept up and running
- Fully customizable and built on AWS products and services

column1: Where are the resources that Elastic Beanstalk provisions created?
column2:
- In your own AWS account
- You can see them under their respective services/resources

column1: Which platforms does Elastic Beanstalk natively support?
column2:
- Go, Java SE, Tomcat
- .NET Core (Linux and Windows)
- Node.js, PHP, Python, Ruby

column1: What Docker options does Elastic Beanstalk offer?
column2:
- Single container Docker
- Multi-container Docker (uses ECS behind the scenes)
- Preconfigured Docker: a way EB supports things before they are natively supported by EB
- Use Docker for any platform not natively supported by EB

column1: How are custom platforms created for Elastic Beanstalk?
column2: - Custom platforms are built via Packer

column1: What is an Elastic Beanstalk Application?
column2:
- A collection of things relating to an application
- Acts as a top-level container/folder for application versions and environments

column1: What is an Elastic Beanstalk Application Version, and what is a source bundle?
column2:
- Application Version: a specific labeled version of deployable code for an application
- Source bundle: the ZIP or WAR file that holds an application version

column1: What is an Elastic Beanstalk Environment?
column2:
- A container of infrastructure and configuration for a specific application version
- A subcontainer inside the Application container
- Environments actually contain the infrastructure
- Each environment is either a web server tier or a worker tier

column1: What is the difference between the web server tier and the worker tier in Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- Web server tier: communicates with end users and accepts their traffic
- Worker tier: processes work passed on from the web tier

column1: How do the Elastic Beanstalk web and worker tiers communicate, and what does each scale on?
column2:
- They communicate via SQS queues: the web tier passes workloads into an SQS queue as messages, and the worker tier receives them
- Web tier scales based on incoming requests to its load balancer
- Worker tier scales based on the number of messages in the SQS queue

column1: What infrastructure does each Elastic Beanstalk environment use?
column2:
- An Auto Scaling group per environment
- Web tier accepts customer connections via an Elastic Load Balancer (ELB)

column1: Where should databases be provisioned when using Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- (Almost) always provision and maintain DBs OUTSIDE of EB
- You can point EB at DBs outside of EB
- You can technically create DBs inside EB, but the DB is lost if the environment is deleted

column1: Which Elastic Beanstalk console sections show provisioning activity, per-instance logs, and health?
column2:
- Events: all of the resources provisioning for the EB application
- Logs: logs for each EC2 instance in the environment
- Health: overall health and individual instance health

column1: What environment presets are available when creating an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
column2:
- Single instance (free tier eligible)
- Single instance (using Spot Instances)
- High availability: 1-4 instances, configured to automatically recover if any instance fails
- High availability (Spot & On-Demand): either On-Demand only or a mix of Spot/On-Demand
- Custom configuration

column1: Which load balancer types can an Elastic Beanstalk environment use?
column2:
- Application Load Balancer: application layer, routes HTTP and HTTPS traffic based on protocol, port, and route
- Classic Load Balancer: previous generation, HTTP, HTTPS, and TCP
- Network Load Balancer: ultra-high performance and static IP addresses
- Can be dedicated to the EB environment or an existing load balancer in your account

column1: How does the Elastic Beanstalk All at once deployment policy work?
column2:
- Deploys to all instances at once
- Causes a brief outage
- Good for test environments

column1: How does the Elastic Beanstalk Rolling deployment policy work, and what are its trade-offs?
column2:
- Deploys in rolling batches; batch size is customizable (>= 1) based on how many instances you can tolerate being offline
- Waits for the current batch to finish and pass health checks before the next batch
- Loss in capacity, because instances are removed from service while being upgraded
- Two versions run at the same time

column1: How does Rolling with additional batch differ from Rolling in Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- Same as Rolling, but with an extra batch to maintain capacity during the process
- Better for production: customers won't see a drop in capacity
- Takes longer and costs more, but is safer
- Two versions run at the same time

column1: How does the Elastic Beanstalk Immutable deployment policy work?
column2:
- A new temporary Auto Scaling group is created with new instances running the new app version
- Once the new instances pass health checks, they are moved to the original ASG, the original instances are terminated, and the temp ASG is removed
- Higher cost (double the instances), but easiest to roll back since the original instances are untouched until deployment completes

column1: How does the Elastic Beanstalk Traffic splitting deployment policy work?
column2:
- Same idea as Immutable: a new temp ASG with fresh instances running the new version
- Adds control over how traffic is distributed between the old and new version
- Allows A/B testing of versions
- No capacity drops

column1: How does Blue/green deployment work with Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- Two separate environments (version A and version B) run in parallel
- Test in the offline environment before switching DNS to the new active stack
- Secondary environment can be kept running as long as you want
- Switching the DNS record between environments makes rollbacks simple

column1: Which Elastic Beanstalk deployment policy suits test environments, and which suits production?
column2:
- Test environments: All at once (fast, brief outage acceptable)
- Production: Rolling with additional batch (no drop in capacity, safer, but slower and costlier)

column1: What happens to an RDS instance created inside an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
column2:
- Its lifecycle is linked to the environment: deleting the environment deletes the DB
- Different EB environments mean different DBs and different data
- Application code can read connection details from environment properties: `RDS_HOSTNAME`, `RDS_PORT`, `RDS_DB_NAME`, `RDS_USERNAME`, `RDS_PASSWORD`

column1: How do you connect an Elastic Beanstalk environment to an RDS instance created outside EB?
column2:
- Manually create the environment properties (`RDS_HOSTNAME`, `RDS_PORT`, `RDS_DB_NAME`, `RDS_USERNAME`, `RDS_PASSWORD`) to point at the RDS instance
- Environments can be swapped out at will because the data is outside the environment's lifecycle

column1: What are the steps to decouple an RDS instance created within Elastic Beanstalk from its environment?
column2:
- 1. Create an RDS snapshot
- 2. Enable deletion protection
- 3. Create a new EB environment with the same app version
- 4. Ensure the new environment can connect to the existing DB (environment properties, security groups, etc.)
- 5. Swap environments (CNAME or DNS)
- 6. Terminate the old environment (it tries to delete the RDS instance but deletion protection blocks it)
- 7. In CloudFormation, find the DELETE_FAILED stack and delete it, choosing to retain the stuck resources

column1: Why is deletion protection enabled when decoupling an RDS instance from an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
column2:
- The old environment's termination will TRY to terminate the RDS instance because their lifecycles are linked
- Deletion protection makes that fail, so the environment is removed but the RDS instance remains

column1: How does Elastic Beanstalk provision infrastructure behind the scenes?
column2: - It uses CloudFormation; you can see the stacks in CloudFormation

column1: What are `.ebextensions` and how are they used?
column2:
- A way to customize Elastic Beanstalk environments
- Add an `.ebextensions` folder inside the app source bundle (ZIP or WAR)
- Files in that folder ending in `.config` are treated as config files
- Files use CloudFormation format to create additional resources in the environment

column1: What configuration elements can be used in `.ebextensions` `.config` files?
column2:
- `option_settings`: set options of resources
- `Resources`: create entirely new resources
- Also introduced in CFN-INIT: `packages`, `sources`, `files`, `users`, `groups`, `container_commands`, `services`

column1: What is required to use HTTPS with Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- 1. Apply an SSL certificate to the load balancer (manually in the console via environment > load balancer configuration, or via `.ebextensions`)
- 2. Configure the security group (manually or via `.ebextensions`): allow port 443 to the load balancer, and allow the load balancer to connect to the instances on the relevant ports

column1: What does cloning an Elastic Beanstalk environment do?
column2:
- Use cases: copy a prod environment to a test environment, or try a new version of a platform branch
- Copies options, environment variables, resources, and other settings
- Copies any RDS in the environment, BUT the data is NOT copied (you must migrate the data yourself)

column1: What can you modify when cloning an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
column2:
- No other changes can be made during the copy (make updates afterwards)
- Exceptions: environment name, environment URL, description, platform version (NOT platform branch), and the service role

column1: What is NOT copied when cloning an Elastic Beanstalk environment?
column2:
- Data in RDS
- Unmanaged changes: changes made to infrastructure using tools other than the EB console/CLI/API (e.g. manually modifying an EC2 instance)

column1: Can you clone an Elastic Beanstalk environment to a different platform branch?
column2:
- No: you can only clone to a different platform version of the same platform branch (a different branch isn't guaranteed to be compatible)
- To use a different platform branch: manually create a new environment, deploy the app code, and make any necessary code changes to ensure it functions correctly

column1: How does single container Docker work in Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- Referred to as "Docker" in the console UI
- Creates one container on a single EC2 instance (1 container per Docker host)
- Uses EC2, NOT ECS

column1: What extra configuration files can single container Docker in Elastic Beanstalk use?
column2:
- You must provide at least one
- `Dockerfile`: EB builds the Docker image and runs a container (use to cleanly build a container within EB)
- `Dockerrun.aws.json` (version 1): use an existing Docker image and configure image, ports, volumes, and other Docker attributes
- `docker-compose.yml`: if you use Docker Compose

column1: How does multi-container Docker mode work in Elastic Beanstalk?
column2:
- Creates an ECS cluster and runs multiple containers per EC2 instance
- EC2 instances are provisioned in the cluster, plus an ELB for high availability
- Requires a `Dockerrun.aws.json` (version 2) file at the root level of the application source bundle
- Images must be stored in a container registry (like ECR)
